title: var, let, and const
description: Differences in scoping and reassignment rules between the three declaration keywords.

blocks.title: Function Scope vs Block Scope
blocks.content: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of `undefined`. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and live in the temporal dead zone until their declaration line executes. `const` additionally forbids reassignment of the binding (though object/array contents can still be mutated).
keyPoints: `var` leaks out of `if`/`for` blocks into the enclosing function scope.
`let`/`const` are confined to the nearest enclosing `{}` block.
`const` prevents rebinding the variable, not mutation of its contents.

blocks.question: What is the difference between let, const, and var?
blocks.answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialized to undefined; let and const are block-scoped and stay in the temporal dead zone until declared; const cannot be reassigned after initialization.
blocks.explanation: Interviewers usually follow up by asking for the classic var-in-a-loop-with-setTimeout gotcha, which let solves naturally by creating a new binding per iteration.

blocks.question: Does this throw an error?
blocks.explanation: `const` only freezes the *binding* — you can never reassign `user` to a different object — but it does nothing to protect the object's contents. Mutating or adding properties is unrelated to const/let/var; to actually make the object immutable you'd need `Object.freeze(user)` (which is shallow) or a deep-freeze utility.

title: Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
description: How declarations are processed before code executes.

blocks.content: During the compile phase, JavaScript registers `var` declarations and function declarations in their scope before execution begins. `let`/`const` declarations are also registered but remain uninitialized — accessing them before their declaration line throws a ReferenceError instead of returning undefined.
keyPoints: Function declarations are fully hoisted, including their body.
Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to `var`/`let` are not callable before the assignment line.
The gap between entering scope and the declaration line is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

blocks.explanation: `a` is hoisted and initialized to undefined, while `b` exists in the TDZ and throws when read before its declaration.

blocks.question: What does this print?
blocks.explanation: `sayHi` is a var, so it is hoisted and initialized to undefined before the assignment runs; `typeof` on undefined returns the string "undefined", not an error.

blocks.question: Is a `class` declaration hoisted the same way a `function` declaration is?
blocks.answer: No — class declarations are hoisted but, like let/const, remain in the Temporal Dead Zone until evaluated. Referencing a class before its declaration line throws a ReferenceError, even though the class 'exists' in scope from the top of the block.
blocks.explanation: This trips people up because `class` looks like it should behave like `function` (both define reusable behavior), but under the hood a class declaration follows let/const hoisting semantics, not function hoisting semantics.

title: Closures
description: Understand lexical scope and closures in JavaScript.

blocks.title: What is a Closure?
blocks.content: A closure is created when a function remembers variables from its lexical scope even after the outer function has completed.
keyPoints: Closures depend on lexical scope.
Inner functions can access outer function variables.
Closures are commonly used for encapsulation and state.

blocks.explanation: The returned function keeps access to the count variable even after createCounter has returned.

blocks.question: What will be printed?
blocks.explanation: var is function-scoped. All callbacks reference the same variable i, whose value is 3 when the callbacks execute.

blocks.mistake: Using `var` in a loop that schedules callbacks and expecting each callback to see its own loop index.
blocks.whyItHappens: All callbacks close over the single shared function-scoped `var` binding.
blocks.correctApproach: Use `let` (creates a fresh binding per iteration) or wrap the body in an IIFE that captures the current value explicitly.

blocks.question: How would you use a closure to create a `createBankAccount(initialBalance)` function whose returned object exposes `deposit()`, `withdraw()`, and `getBalance()`, but with no way for outside code to directly read or overwrite the balance variable?
blocks.explanation: This is the module/revealing pattern: `balance` lives only in createBankAccount's scope, and the three returned functions close over it. There is no `this.balance` property anywhere, so the caller has no way to reach in and set `balance` directly — the only surface area is the methods you chose to expose. This predates (and still coexists with) ES class private fields (`#balance`) as a way to achieve real encapsulation.

title: The Event Loop
description: How the call stack, task queue, and microtask queue coordinate to run asynchronous code.

blocks.title: Call Stack, Microtasks, Macrotasks
blocks.content: JavaScript runs on a single call stack. Once the stack is empty, the event loop first drains the entire microtask queue (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) before running a single macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering).
keyPoints: All microtasks queued run before the next macrotask, even ones queued while draining the microtask queue.
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` never runs immediately — it waits for the current synchronous code and the entire microtask queue to finish.
Long-running synchronous code blocks the event loop entirely, freezing the UI.

blocks.question: What is the logged order?
blocks.explanation: Synchronous code (1, 4) runs first. The microtask queue (Promise .then, logging 3) drains next. Only then does the macrotask queue run the setTimeout callback (2).

blocks.question: Can a chain of Promise.then() callbacks starve setTimeout callbacks from ever running?
blocks.answer: Yes, in principle — if each .then() callback keeps enqueuing another microtask, the engine keeps draining the microtask queue and never reaches the macrotask queue.
blocks.explanation: This is a well-known way to explain why microtasks can 'starve' macrotasks; in practice this shows up as recursive Promise chains freezing timer-based code.

blocks.question: Where does requestAnimationFrame fit relative to microtasks and macrotasks?
blocks.answer: requestAnimationFrame callbacks run before the browser's next repaint, after the current task and all queued microtasks have drained, but they are scheduled separately from the setTimeout/setInterval macrotask queue — the browser tries to run them right before it paints the frame.
blocks.explanation: In practice, the ordering for a single tick looks like: synchronous code → all microtasks → requestAnimationFrame callbacks (right before paint) → paint → next macrotask. This is why requestAnimationFrame, not setTimeout(fn, 16), is the correct tool for visual/animation updates — it's synchronized to the browser's actual render cycle.

title: Promises and async/await
description: Modeling asynchronous operations without callback pyramids.

blocks.content: A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never, with three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. `async/await` is syntax sugar over Promises that lets asynchronous code read like synchronous code, with `try/catch` handling rejections.
keyPoints: An `async function` always returns a Promise, even if you `return` a plain value.
`await` pauses the async function (not the whole thread) until the awaited Promise settles.
Unhandled Promise rejections should be caught with `try/catch` around `await`, or `.catch()` on the Promise chain.

blocks.explanation: Errors from either the fetch call or a non-OK response are funneled into the same catch block.

blocks.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, and Promise.race?
blocks.answer: Promise.all rejects immediately if any promise rejects; Promise.allSettled always resolves with the outcome (fulfilled/rejected) of every promise; Promise.race settles as soon as the first promise settles, whether fulfilled or rejected.
blocks.explanation: Use allSettled when you need every result regardless of individual failures, and race for timeout patterns (racing a request against a timer).

blocks.question: What is logged, and in what order?
blocks.explanation: A `throw` inside an async function doesn't throw synchronously to the caller — it rejects the Promise that function returns. `run()` starts executing synchronously up to `await getData()`, which suspends it (control returns to the caller, so "after" logs before anything from inside run() resumes), and only once the rejected Promise is processed as a microtask does the `catch` block run and log last. This is exactly why `try/catch` around `await` works: await converts a Promise rejection back into a synchronously-catchable throw, just deferred to the microtask queue.

title: Prototypes and the Prototype Chain
description: How JavaScript objects inherit properties and methods.

blocks.content: Every JavaScript object has an internal [[Prototype]] link (exposed as `__proto__` or via `Object.getPrototypeOf`). Property lookups walk up this chain until the property is found or the chain ends at `null`. `class` syntax is sugar over this same prototype-based inheritance.
keyPoints: Methods defined in a class body live on `ClassName.prototype`, shared by all instances.
`Object.create(proto)` creates an object whose prototype is explicitly `proto`.
Own properties shadow prototype properties with the same name.

blocks.question: What does this print?
blocks.explanation: `dog` does not have its own `speak` property, so the lookup walks up to `Animal.prototype.speak`, which uses `this.name` bound to `dog`.

blocks.question: What's the difference between `Object.hasOwn(obj, 'key')` (or `obj.hasOwnProperty('key')`) and the `'key' in obj` operator?
blocks.answer: `hasOwnProperty`/`Object.hasOwn` check only the object's own properties, ignoring the prototype chain. The `in` operator checks the own properties *and* everything inherited up the prototype chain.
blocks.explanation: This matters when iterating: `for...in` walks enumerable properties including inherited ones, which is why it's common (and recommended) to guard the loop body with `if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key))` to avoid accidentally processing inherited properties like custom methods added to Object.prototype by a poorly-behaved library.

title: Understanding this, call, apply, and bind
description: How the value of `this` is determined at call time, and how to control it explicitly.

blocks.content: `this` is determined by how a function is called, not where it is defined — except for arrow functions, which capture `this` lexically from their enclosing scope at creation time. `call`/`apply` invoke a function immediately with an explicit `this`; `bind` returns a new function permanently bound to a given `this`.
keyPoints: Plain function call: `this` is undefined in strict mode, or the global object otherwise.
Method call (`obj.method()`): `this` is `obj`.
Arrow functions never have their own `this` — they inherit it from the enclosing lexical scope.

blocks.question: A method is detached from its object and passed as a callback, e.g. `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)`. What happens to `this` inside method?
blocks.answer: `this` is no longer `obj` — it becomes undefined (strict mode) or the global object, because the function is now called without a receiver.
blocks.explanation: This is why event handlers and callbacks are often written as arrow functions or explicitly bound: `setTimeout(obj.method.bind(obj), 100)` or `setTimeout(() => obj.method(), 100)`.

blocks.question: What does this log, and why?
blocks.answer: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'count').
blocks.explanation: `increment` is a regular class method, so its `this` depends on the call site — assigning it to `handler` and calling `handler()` invokes it with no receiver, so `this` is undefined in strict mode (all class bodies are implicitly strict). The fix is either an arrow-function class field (`increment = () => { this.count++; ... }`, which captures `this` lexically at construction time) or explicitly binding: `const handler = counter.increment.bind(counter)`.
hints: This exact bug is why UI framework code (event handlers, callback props) so often uses arrow-function class fields.

title: Debounce and Throttle
description: Rate-limiting patterns for expensive or frequent event handlers.

blocks.content: Debounce delays invoking a function until a burst of calls has stopped for a given period — ideal for search-as-you-type. Throttle guarantees a function runs at most once per fixed interval regardless of how many times it's triggered — ideal for scroll or resize handlers.
keyPoints: Debounce: wait for silence (e.g. 300ms with no new keystrokes) before firing.
Throttle: fire immediately, then ignore further calls until the interval elapses.
Both patterns reduce the number of expensive operations (API calls, layout reads) triggered by rapid-fire events.

blocks.explanation: Every new call cancels the pending timer and schedules a fresh one, so `fn` only runs once the calls stop for `delay` milliseconds.

blocks.question: Would you use debounce or throttle for a live search box that calls an API as the user types?
blocks.explanation: You only want to call the API once the user pauses typing; firing on a fixed interval (throttle) would still send requests for incomplete, transient search terms.

blocks.question: Implement a `throttle(fn, limit)` function: fn should run immediately on the first call, then ignore further calls until `limit` milliseconds have passed.
blocks.explanation: Unlike debounce (which always waits for a quiet period), this 'leading-edge' throttle fires right away for responsiveness, then uses a boolean flag and a single timer to block every subsequent call until the cooldown window elapses — a good fit for scroll/resize handlers where you want at least one immediate reaction, followed by a capped rate.
